title: Trump Backs Iraq's Anti-Smuggling Drive as Baghdad Seizes Kurdish Crossings
excerpt: Washington aligns with Prime Minister al-Zaidi as Baghdad declares non-SOMO crude exports smuggling, closes two Kurdish crossings and claims $100 billion in losses since 2008.
body:
• President Donald Trump on Friday publicly backed Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's campaign to stop oil smuggling, end corruption and bring all weapons under exclusive state control.
  • Baghdad this week moved to seize control of the Kurdish region's border crossings and oilfields, closed two crossings with Syria and Iran, and declared crude exports bypassing state marketer SOMO to be smuggling.
  • Iraq's government says oil smuggled through the Kurdish region cost the treasury an estimated $100 billion between 2008 and 2025; Kurdish leaders call the federal moves unconstitutional, and Baghdad-Erbil talks are set for December 1.
  • The confrontation also squeezes Iran: Iraq is Tehran's main land outlet under blockade, and the crackdown began with a standoff against the Iran-backed Kataib Hezbollah militia.

US President Donald Trump on Friday backed Iraq's efforts to assert control over its oil resources and armed groups, aligning Washington openly with Baghdad in a showdown that pits the federal government against both the semi-autonomous Kurdish region and the country's Iran-backed militias.

"We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state."

— Donald Trump, US President, on Truth Social

"We support Prime Minister al-Zaidi's efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions," Trump added in the Truth Social post, according to CNN. Al-Zaidi, a 41-year-old businessman who took power in May, launched an anti-corruption campaign on taking office that seeks to consolidate both oil and arms under state control. Trump welcomed him at the White House in July, calling him "a great fighter" and "a great fan of America."

A week of escalation in the north

The endorsement, Washington's first comment on the Baghdad-Erbil tensions, capped a rapid sequence of federal moves. On Tuesday, al-Zaidi moved to place the Kurdish region's border crossings and several oilfields under federal control. On Wednesday, Iraq's top court ruled that Baghdad can deploy federal forces along all of the country's international borders, including those in the Kurdistan region. On Thursday, Iraq closed two crossings in the region, one with Syria and one with Iran, and demonstrations broke out in the Kurdish region over what its leaders view as an infringement of their rights.

On Friday, state media reported that Iraq had declared the export of crude outside the state oil company SOMO to be "smuggling," because the revenues do not enter the state treasury. Government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said Iraq estimates it lost more than $100 billion between 2008 and 2025 to oil exported from the Kurdistan Region. Al Jazeera noted that Reuters reported it was unclear how that figure had been calculated.

Kurdish leaders have rejected the measures. Kurdistan Region Prime Minister Masrour Barzani called them unconstitutional, and the region's two main parties issued a rare joint statement protesting Baghdad's takeover of oil fields and border crossings as "a red line," the Erbil-based broadcaster Rudaw said. Kurdish officials have said they do not want clashes with Baghdad and have left the door open to talks; a meeting between Baghdad and Erbil is due on December 1 under the sponsorship of the head of Iraq's Supreme Judicial Council.

The campaign began against a militia

The anti-smuggling drive did not start in the north. It began in Jurf al-Sakhar, a town south of Baghdad that the Iran-backed group Kataib Hezbollah has held since 2014. Senior Iraqi security and oil officials told Reuters the group has run an oil smuggling network there, siphoning state-owned crude worth hundreds of millions of dollars since 2021; Kataib Hezbollah denies the allegations. Al-Zaidi gave the group until November 20 to leave the town, and a compromise reached a day before the deadline put government forces into Jurf al-Sakhar under a joint operations centre, with the group's units due to withdraw gradually.

The militia file remains open. Kataib Hezbollah is not the only group resisting disarmament — Harakat al-Nujaba and Kataib Sayyid al-Shuhada have also refused — and after armed groups missed a September 30 deadline to hand over their weapons, the government pushed the deadline back to June 2027.

Why Washington is leaning in

Analysts say the timing of Trump's post is the message. Salim Zakhour, a researcher in constitutional law, told Al Jazeera the post tells Kurdish leaders "that all the measures taken by the federal government have strong American backing." Muhanad Seloom of the Middle East Council on Global Affairs described Iraq as "the land gap" in Trump's blockade of Iran: Iraqi buyers imported about $11.9 billion of Iranian goods in 2024, Iranian gas fuels power plants producing 30 to 40 percent of Iraq's electricity, and US Treasury designations since July 2023 describe schemes in which Iranian oil is relabelled as Iraqi. Washington also holds unusual leverage because Iraq's oil revenues are held at the Federal Reserve Bank of New York.

Tehran has noticed. Mohammad Mokhber, an adviser to Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, warned Iraq on Saturday against becoming a "tool" for Trump's policies. The December 1 talks in Baghdad are now the next test: whether Erbil accepts the court's ruling on border control, and whether al-Zaidi's campaign can hold both fronts — Kurdish and militia — at once.
